item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=31Lf2DmMD5c

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析西藏與歷代中原王朝的政治與宗教關係，釐清「自古以來」論述的歷史爭議。
  • 完整梳理1911年至1951年間西藏發行貨幣、辦理外交等實質獨立狀態的具體實踐。
  • 以作者親訪達蘭薩拉的田野觀察視角切入，提供跳脫傳統單一敘事的多元歷史維度。

摘要

從觀光熱潮到流亡重鎮：達蘭薩拉的見聞

作者指出，當代大眾前往西藏旅遊已形成風潮，但多數人對達賴喇嘛流亡印度及1959年拉薩事件的歷史背景缺乏了解。為探尋西藏的過往與現狀，作者親赴印度北部山城達蘭薩拉（又稱「小拉薩」），實地走訪聚集數萬藏人與流亡政府的所在地，並藉此檢視中共關於「西藏自古屬於中國」以及「十七條協議」等歷史敘事。

解構「自古以來」：唐元明清與西藏的真實互動

針對官方宣稱西藏「自古以來」屬於中國的論調，作者回顧了歷代歷史。唐代時期，吐蕃帝國實力足以與唐朝分庭抗禮，拉薩大昭寺前立於823年的《唐蕃會盟碑》便明文記載兩國各自劃定邊界、互為對等國家。元代蒙古人統治時，雙方形成提供庇護與福田的「供施關係」，並非主權管轄；若依征服邏輯，反而是中原與西藏同遭蒙古征服。明朝從未在西藏駐軍或徵稅，而清朝雖於18世紀擊退準噶爾後設置駐藏大臣並推行金瓶掣籤，但事務劃歸理藩院處理，屬於滿洲大汗對藩屬的保護關係，非等同於內地十八省的直接統治。

實質獨立的四十年：1911至1951年的西藏主權實踐

作者強調，1911年辛亥革命爆發至1951年間是理解西藏問題的關鍵階段。清帝國覆滅後，駐藏清軍被遣返，第十三世達賴喇嘛於1913年發表公告闡明西藏為獨立國家，並與蒙古簽署條約互相承認主權。在此期間，西藏發行獨立的貨幣與郵票、設立外交局、在二戰中宣布中立，且西藏代表團曾持西藏政府核發的護照獲得英美等國簽證。即便國民政府派員前往拉薩，亦僅以賓客身分列席儀式，直至1949年國民政府人員全面遭西藏驅逐，西藏在長達四十年間維持著實質獨立的政治運作。

武力逼和與十七條協議：歷史轉折與制度承諾

1950年10月，中共解放軍渡過金沙江發動昌都戰役，重創西藏軍隊主力。面對軍事懸殊，西藏代表團於1951年5月在北京簽署《十七條協議》。作者分析指出，該協議在條文中曾明文承諾實行民族區域自治、不變更西藏原有的政治制度，並保障達賴喇嘛的地位與職權不被更改，其承諾形式與後續香港「一國兩制」的歷史演變具有極高的相似性。

================================================

In 2025, the number of tourists. visiting Tibet reached 70.73 million,. while the total population of Tibet is. only 3.74 million. You have to scramble. for Potala Palace tickets in advance,. and traffic jams are common on National. Highway 318 into Tibet. You even have. to queue up to take a picture at scenic. spots. Chinese people have a special. affection for Tibet, seeing it as a. pure land where a trip can cleanse the. soul. Many people simply call traveling. to Tibet a "pilgrimage," but if you. were to ask these tens of millions of. people one question: Why does the Dalai. Lama live in India? I estimate that. nine out of ten wouldn't be able to. answer, and the remaining one might. tell you it's because he is a wicked. separatist. If you ask one more. question: What actually happened in. Lhasa in 1959? Basically, very few. people truly know. For the past two. weeks, I have been to India. Actually,. I was just passing through the capital,. New Delhi; my real destination was a. small town at the foot of the Himalayas. in northern India called Dharamshala. Starting from New Delhi, it's no. exaggeration to say it was a grueling. journey; the car drove for ten hours,. and the final stretch was a winding. mountain road at an altitude of 2,000. meters. When I arrived, I was dizzy. This town has the nickname "Little. Lhasa," home to tens of thousands of. Tibetans. They even have a government. —a government-in-exile that has lost. its homeland since 1959. I attended a. seminar there and stayed for several. days, finally having the chance to. personally understand their past and. present. In the last episode, I talked. about the amazing India I saw, and. today, we...Does the CCP's claim that " Tibet has been part of China since. ancient times" have any basis in. reality? What exactly is the story. behind the so-called "liberation of a. million serfs"? And how should we view. the Tibet of today and the Tibet in. exile? There is a phrase everyone has. likely heard, as I just mentioned: that. it has been Chinese territory since. ancient times. Chinese people don't. even think twice about it and believe. it deeply. If we look at the history of. Tibet, starting from the Tibetan Empire. in the 7th century, what was the. Tibetan Empire back then? It was an. empire that could sit on equal footing. with the Tang Dynasty. In 763 AD, the. Tibetan army even once invaded Chang'an. , scaring Emperor Daizong away. In 821. AD, the Tang and Tibet formed an. alliance in Chang'an, renewed it in. Lhasa the following year, and erected a. stele in 823 AD. This stele still. stands today at the entrance of the. Jokhang Temple in Lhasa, known as the. Tang-Tibet Alliance Stele. It is. inscribed in both Chinese and Tibetan,. stating that the Tibetan kingdom is at. peace and the Chinese kingdom is at. ease, each respecting its own borders. This is the earliest surviving official. document regarding the status of Tibet. It explicitly writes about two. countries and defines the border. between them. If you are looking for. evidence that Tibet has not been part. of Chinese territory since ancient. times, this stele is the best proof. The Tubo dynasty collapsed in the 9th. century. Tibet remained fragmented for. several centuries until the Mongols. arrived. There was a patron-priest. relationship between the Mongols and. the Tibetans. The Mongol Great Khan was. the patron, and the Tibetan Lama was. the merit field; one provided troops. and money, while the other chanted. prayers for blessings. This. relationship did not involve. sovereignty. Yet, the CCP claims that. from then on, Tibet became a part of. China. This claim was written into the. first white paper on the Tibet issue in. 1992. The original text states that in. the mid-13th century, Tibet was. formally incorporated into the. territory of the Chinese Yuan Dynasty. Just think about it: the Mongols did. not just conquer Tibet; they first. conquered the Central Plains dynasties. The Southern Song Dynasty was wiped out. by the Mongols. If we follow the CCP's. later logic, we should say that in the. mid-13th century, China was formally. incorporated into the Mongol territory,. so China has been a part of Mongolia. since ancient times. Later Chinese. white papers changed this narrative,. adding the four words "since ancient. times." It seems they realized that the. Yuan Dynasty argument was not strong. enough on its own. During the Ming. Dynasty, the court never stationed a. single soldier, collected a single cent. of tax, or appointed a single official. in Tibet. It wasn't until the 18th. century that Tibet had any tributary. relationship with the Qing Dynasty. In. 1720, the Kangxi Emperor’s army.

entered Lhasa and drove out the. Dzungars. In 1727, they began. appointing the Resident Commissioners. in Tibet. In 1793, the Qianlong Emperor. established the Golden Urn system. However, this control still did not. amount to sovereignty, because the. Resident Commissioners were overseen by. the Lifan Yuan. The Lifan Yuan managed. Mongolia, Tibet, and the Muslim regions. . These areas were dependencies held by. the Qing Emperor in his capacity as the. Great Khan and the incarnation of. Manjushri. This was an entirely. different system and matter from his. role as the Emperor of China governing. the eighteen provinces of Han China. Furthermore, the Qing only sought. symbolic authority and never directly. ruled Tibet. By the 19th century, this. protectorate relationship had vanished,. and the Resident Commissioners in Lhasa. existed in name only. Therefore, if we. truly want to respect history, we. should understand that the phrase " since ancient times" simply does not. hold water. In the Tang Dynasty, it was. a relationship between two countries; in the Yuan, it was the Mongol conquest. of both; and in the Ming, it was merely. nominal titles. The Qing Dynasty was. merely a nominal suzerain, yet China. has compressed this complex history. into the four words "since ancient. times," brainwashing over a billion. people for decades. The 40-year period. from 1911 to 1951 is the key to the. entire issue. In 1904, the British led. troops into Lhasa and forced Tibet to. sign the Lhasa Convention; note that. this was a treaty between Britain and. Tibet. In 1905, the Qing Dynasty sent. Zhao Erfeng into the Kham region, where. he killed people and burned monasteries. . In 1910, the Qing entered Lhasa again. , and the 13th Dalai Lama fled to India. . In 1912, the Xinhai Revolution. succeeded, the Qing Empire collapsed,. and the Qing troops in Lhasa were. disarmed and sent back to China. In. early 1913, the 13th Dalai Lama. returned to Lhasa and issued a. proclamation formally clarifying the. relationship between Tibet and China,. stating that it had been a. patron-priest relationship, not one of. subordination. He said, "We are a small. , religious, and independent nation." That same year, Tibet and Mongolia. signed a treaty in Urga, mutually. recognizing each other as independent. states. Over the next few decades,. Tibet continued to exercise its. independent sovereignty. In 1913, it. began issuing its own currency, and. later it had its own stamps. In 1924,. it opened an English school, and in. 1942, it established a foreign office; between 1913 and 1914, Britain, China,. and Tibet held a conference in Simla,. India, to define borders, and the. Chinese representative Chen Yifan. signed the draft treaty. However,. Beijing later reneged and refused to. recognize it. From 1917 to 1918, the. Tibetan army fought Qing and Sichuan. forces and recovered Chamdo; they. fought again from 1930 to 1932, this. time against Sichuan warlord Liu Wenhui. and Qinghai warlord Ma Bufang; during. WWII, Tibet declared neutrality and, in. 1942, refused China’s request to. build a road through Tibet from India. The U.S. Office of Strategic Services. even specifically sent personnel to. Lhasa for negotiations. In 1947, Tibet. sent a trade delegation abroad, led by. Tsepon Shakabpa, who carried a passport. issued by the Tibetan government,. bearing visas from the United States,. Britain, India, France, Italy, and. Switzerland. Even today, the U.S. Department of State's own diplomatic. archives record the issuance of a visa. to a Tibetan passport in 1948. Of. course. The Republican government. shared the same imperialist mindset as. the Qing Empire; neither would abandon. their territorial ambitions toward. Tibet. In 1933, when the 13th Dalai. Lama passed away and Nanjing sent Huang. Musong to Tibet, the Tibetan side. clearly told him, "We do not accept. Chinese sovereignty." In 1940, when the. 14th Dalai Lama was enthroned, Nanjing. sent Wu Zhongxin, Chairman of the. Mongolian and Tibetan Affairs. Commission. The official Republic of. China narrative claims Wu Zhongxin. presided over the ceremony, but in. reality, he just attended as a guest,. sitting to the side and playing no. actual role. In July 1949, as the. Nationalist government retreated during. the Civil War, Tibet expelled all. personnel from the Republic of China's. Lhasa office. In short, from 1913 to. 1951, Tibet existed as a de facto. independent state. Finally, the CCP. arrived. On October 6, 1950, the PLA. crossed the Jinsha River, and by the. 19th, they had captured Qamdo. The 18th. Army mobilized 40,000 troops, with over. 20,000 actually engaged, while the.

Tibetan army only had about 8,000. With. Qamdo lost, Lhasa had no power to. resist. On May 23, 1951, the Tibetan. delegation signed a Seventeen-Point. Agreement under military duress. You. can still find the full text of this. agreement online today; I suggest. reading it, as it is strikingly similar. to what happened later in Hong Kong. Article 3 states that the Tibetan. people have the right to exercise. national regional autonomy. Article 4. states that the central government will. not change the existing political. system in Tibet. The Dalai Lama's. status and authority will not be. altered, and Article 7 grants religious. freedom, respects the customs and. beliefs of the Tibetan people, and. guarantees that temple income will not. be changed. Article 11 adds that the. central government will not force. reforms in Tibet, hoping instead that. the local government will carry them. out voluntarily. Tibet kept its. original government, systems, and. religion; it merely acknowledged the. central government's sovereignty. Isn't. this just the "One Country, Two Systems. " policy that came later? It predates. Hong Kong, but this agreement had a. major flaw from the very beginning. The. "Tibet" it refers to was only the small. area directly administered by the Dalai. Lama's government. This corresponds to. the borders of today’s Tibet. Autonomous Region, yet the Tibetan. people live in areas far beyond that. Kham and Amdo—today's Tibetan regions. in Sichuan, Qinghai, and southern Gansu. —are home to more than half of the. Tibetan population and were. historically part of the Tibetan Empire. . As a result, beginning in 1955, the. CCP launched violent struggles and land. reforms in Kham and Amdo, attacking. landlords and seizing temples, which. completely forced the hand of the. Khampa people. In February 1956, Litang. Monastery was surrounded by the CCP. army, with thousands of Tibetans hiding. inside. Sichuan provincial military. records explicitly state that on March. 29, the air force deployed two Tu-4. aircraft to strafe and bomb the site. The Tu-4, a heavy bomber modeled after. the American B-29, saw its first combat. deployment in China against an ancient. monastery, filled with thousands of men. , women, and children. Litang Monastery. dates back to the Wanli era of the Ming. Dynasty, with nearly 400 years of. history and, at its peak, over 4,000. resident monks; it was one of the. largest and most sacred temples in the. Kham region. That spring, over 3,000. people from 47 tribes—men, women, the. elderly, and children—herded their. livestock into the monastery, believing. it to be a sanctuary of peace, right? They thought the army wouldn't attack a. holy place, but the troops surrounded. the monastery and launched an assault. on April 22nd; they failed to take it. the first time, losing 80 men, a. mountain gun, and 68 rifles. And then,. they called in the aircraft. These. nomads had never seen an airplane in. their lives. There wasn't even a word. in the Tibetan language to describe it. They saw a flying metal machine. dropping things from the sky into the. monastery; they had spent their lives. peacefully herding sheep and had no. idea that those things were bombs. At. noon on the 29th, two bombers strafed. and bombed the monastery repeatedly; at. 4:00 AM on the 30th, troops attacked. from three sides, and the entire. monastery was reduced to rubble. Sichuan military records claim they. wiped out 204, killed 311, wounded 80,. and captured 1,613; Air Force records. show that Tu-4 bombers flew 21 sorties. that spring, bombing Litang and several. surrounding monasteries. Of course,. this was just the beginning; by 1958,. the war reached the grasslands of. Qinghai and Gansu, where the iron birds. in the sky were no longer targeting. monasteries, but ordinary fleeing. civilians. Nomadic tribes herded their. livestock toward the south, with. thousands of people and tens of. thousands of animals stretched out in a. long line. Looking down from an. airplane, this was nothing but a large,. slow-moving ground target. Planes. strafed and bombed from the sky; no one. could count how many people died. On. June 1, 1958, the battle report of the. 1st Cavalry Division in Henan County,. Qinghai, claimed to have annihilated. over 1,200 insurgents, yet the same. files stated that over 7,000 were. surrounded, with only 2,000 rifles. seized. Who, then, were the remaining. four or five thousand people? They had. no guns; they were ordinary people. holding prayer wheels and rosaries,. clutching their children. But what. greeted them were the machine guns of. the troops. After the bursts of gunfire. , bodies drifted down the river. A.

Tibetan named Sangye Norbu later wrote. his memoirs, describing the scene on. the grasslands: as far as the eye could. see, there were corpses everywhere,. many of them children, and mothers. lying dead while holding their children. . In Tiechagou, Qinghai, the People's. Liberation Army deployed bombers and. six regiments. So many Tibetans and. livestock died that their bodies rotted. in the gullies; the water flowing from. the mountains stank, and for three. years after the battle, no one dared to. drink it. Among these people, how many. were armed resisters, and how many were. just elderly people, women, and. children following their tribes? Wave. after wave of Tibetan refugees from. Kham fled to Lhasa. The Dalai Lama and. those around him finally realized that. what had happened in the Kham region. would sooner or later happen to them as. well. On March 10, 1959, rumors spread. that the PLA invited the Dalai Lama to. the military district to watch a play,. forbidding him from bringing his guards. . Thousands of Lhasa residents flooded. outside the Norbulingka palace,. surrounding it to prevent him from. leaving, fearing he would fall into a. CCP ambush. On the night of March 17,. the Dalai Lama disguised himself as an. ordinary soldier and left the city. By. dawn on March 20, PLA artillery shells. were raining down on Norbulingka. On. March 28, Zhou Enlai signed a State. Council order announcing the. dissolution of the Tibetan government. From that day on, the CCP officially. tore up the Seventeen-Point Agreement. it had signed and promised to uphold. The Dalai Lama escaped in time,. entering India on March 31. On April 18. , he issued a statement saying that the. agreement had been imposed on Tibet. under the threat of force, and now,. even the CCP itself no longer abided by. it. According to official Chinese. statistics, from 1956 to 1962, the PLA. mobilized 235,000 troops from eight. military regions and conducted over. 10,000 aircraft sorties. The number of. so-called "eliminated" Tibetans was at. least 347,000, accounting for 16%of the. total Tibetan population at the time. In Qinghai province alone, more than. 108,000 people were arrested between. 1958 and 1960. In Qinghai’s detention. centers, over 80,000 of the imprisoned. Tibetans died, a death rate as high as. 54%. Conditions in detention centers in. other regions were similar, with death. rates exceeding half. Compared to 1957,. the population in the Tibetan regions. had decreased by 44%, and the. population in the Golok area had. dropped by 35%—all according to these. official statistics. In 1982, the. Qinghai provincial government itself. exonerated those who had been labeled. as "rebels" back then, rehabilitating a. total of more than 78,000 people, a. proportion as high as 92%. In other. words, the CCP itself admitted that. among the so-called "rebels" it had. struck and eliminated back then, more. than nine out of every ten cases were. wrong. In May 1962, the Panchen Lama. submitted a report to Zhou Enlai, later. known as the "70,000-Character Petition. ." You must realize the Panchen was. supported by the CCP; even he couldn't. stand it anymore. He stated that before. the reforms, Tibet had over 2,500. temples, but after the reforms, only 70. remained, a reduction of 97%. There. were originally 110,000 monks, now only. 7,000 remain, a reduction of 93%. Every. region arrested at least 10,000 people; in some places, the majority of the. male population was locked up. In. Qinghai, people starved to death, with. daily rations only a few ounces; some. had to survive on roots and tree bark. After Mao Zedong read it, his reaction. was the same as when he saw Peng. Dehuai’s report on the border issues,. calling it a "poisonous arrow shot at. the Party." Because of this letter, the. Panchen was denounced. In 1968, he was. thrown into Qincheng Prison, held until. 1977, and after his release, he was. under house arrest until 1982, finally. returning to Shigatse in January 1989. In a public speech, he stated that. Tibet's sacrifice over the past 30. years had been greater than what had. been gained. Five days later, he died. suddenly at the age of 50. The CCP has. two narratives prepared for Tibet. The. first is the so-called "since ancient. times" argument, which I just explained. . The second is that pre-liberation. Tibet was a feudal serfdom system where. religion and politics were unified. 95%. of the people were serfs and slaves,. and serf owners would flay human skin. for thangkas and use human bones for. ritual objects, with an average life. expectancy of only 35.5 years. After. the CCP's 1959 reforms, millions of. serfs rose up to become masters of. their own destiny. In 2019, a "Serf. Liberation Memorial Hall" opened in.

Lhasa, featuring a sculpture group. called "Serf Rage" made in 1975. After. finishing the exhibit, you are left. feeling that the past was nothing short. of hell. You must thank the Communist. Party and thank the People's Liberation. Army. So, do these so-called human skin. thangkas and human bone ritual objects. actually exist? Objectively speaking,. they do. If you understand Tibetan. Buddhism, you know these are no. different in essence from the sarira. relics worshipped in Han Chinese. Buddhism. For example, the Kapala is. made from a human skull, the Kangling. is a trumpet made from a human thigh. bone, and there are bone drums; these. are all Tantric ritual objects, with. bones coming from deceased. practitioners. The Tibetan tradition is. sky burial, where the body is offered. to vultures, and bones are offered to. temples to be crafted into ritual. objects. In their view, this is an act. of immeasurable merit, and one that is. voluntarily pledged during their. lifetime. In 1964, the Communist. government held an exhibition in.   • 深入剖析西藏與歷代中原王朝的政治與宗教關係，釐清「自古以來」論述的歷史爭議。

  • 以作者親訪達蘭薩拉的田野觀察視角切入，提供跳脫傳統單一敘事的多元歷史維度。

摘要

從觀光熱潮到流亡重鎮：達蘭薩拉的見聞

作者指出，當代大眾前往西藏旅遊已形成風潮，但多數人對達賴喇嘛流亡印度及1959年拉薩事件的歷史背景缺乏了解。為探尋西藏的過往與現狀，作者親赴印度北部山城達蘭薩拉（又稱「小拉薩」），實地走訪聚集數萬藏人與流亡政府的所在地，並藉此檢視中共關於「西藏自古屬於中國」以及「十七條協議」等歷史敘事。

解構「自古以來」：唐元明清與西藏的真實互動

針對官方宣稱西藏「自古以來」屬於中國的論調，作者回顧了歷代歷史。唐代時期，吐蕃帝國實力足以與唐朝分庭抗禮，拉薩大昭寺前立於823年的《唐蕃會盟碑》便明文記載兩國各自劃定邊界、互為對等國家。元代蒙古人統治時，雙方形成提供庇護與福田的「供施關係」，並非主權管轄；若依征服邏輯，反而是中原與西藏同遭蒙古征服。明朝從未在西藏駐軍或徵稅，而清朝雖於18世紀擊退準噶爾後設置駐藏大臣並推行金瓶掣籤，但事務劃歸理藩院處理，屬於滿洲大汗對藩屬的保護關係，非等同於內地十八省的直接統治。

實質獨立的四十年：1911至1951年的西藏主權實踐

作者強調，1911年辛亥革命爆發至1951年間是理解西藏問題的關鍵階段。清帝國覆滅後，駐藏清軍被遣返，第十三世達賴喇嘛於1913年發表公告闡明西藏為獨立國家，並與蒙古簽署條約互相承認主權。在此期間，西藏發行獨立的貨幣與郵票、設立外交局、在二戰中宣布中立，且西藏代表團曾持西藏政府核發的護照獲得英美等國簽證。即便國民政府派員前往拉薩，亦僅以賓客身分列席儀式，直至1949年國民政府人員全面遭西藏驅逐，西藏在長達四十年間維持著實質獨立的政治運作。

武力逼和與十七條協議：歷史轉折與制度承諾

1950年10月，中共解放軍渡過金沙江發動昌都戰役，重創西藏軍隊主力。面對軍事懸殊，西藏代表團於1951年5月在北京簽署《十七條協議》。作者分析指出，該協議在條文中曾明文承諾實行民族區域自治、不變更西藏原有的政治制度，並保障達賴喇嘛的地位與職權不被更改，其承諾形式與後續香港「一國兩制」的歷史演變具有極高的相似性。

You. can still find the full text of this. agreement online today; I suggest. reading it, as it is strikingly similar. to what happened later in Hong Kong. Article 3 states that the Tibetan. people have the right to exercise. national regional autonomy. Article 4. states that the central government will. not change the existing political. system in Tibet. The Dalai Lama's. status and authority will not be. altered, and Article 7 grants religious. freedom, respects the customs and. beliefs of the Tibetan people, and. guarantees that temple income will not. be changed. Article 11 adds that the. central government will not force. reforms in Tibet, hoping instead that. the local government will carry them. out voluntarily. Tibet kept its. original government, systems, and. religion; it merely acknowledged the. central government's sovereignty. Isn't. this just the "One Country, Two Systems. " policy that came later? It predates. Hong Kong, but this agreement had a. major flaw from the very beginning. The. "Tibet" it refers to was only the small. area directly administered by the Dalai. Lama's government. This corresponds to. the borders of today’s Tibet. Autonomous Region, yet the Tibetan. people live in areas far beyond that. Kham and Amdo—today's Tibetan regions. in Sichuan, Qinghai, and southern Gansu. —are home to more than half of the. Tibetan population and were. historically part of the Tibetan Empire. . As a result, beginning in 1955, the. CCP launched violent struggles and land. reforms in Kham and Amdo, attacking. landlords and seizing temples, which. completely forced the hand of the. Khampa people. In February 1956, Litang. Monastery was surrounded by the CCP. army, with thousands of Tibetans hiding. inside. Sichuan provincial military. records explicitly state that on March. 29, the air force deployed two Tu-4. aircraft to strafe and bomb the site. The Tu-4, a heavy bomber modeled after. the American B-29, saw its first combat. deployment in China against an ancient. monastery, filled with thousands of men. , women, and children. Litang Monastery. dates back to the Wanli era of the Ming. Dynasty, with nearly 400 years of. history and, at its peak, over 4,000. resident monks; it was one of the. largest and most sacred temples in the. Kham region. That spring, over 3,000. people from 47 tribes—men, women, the. elderly, and children—herded their. livestock into the monastery, believing. it to be a sanctuary of peace, right? They thought the army wouldn't attack a. holy place, but the troops surrounded. the monastery and launched an assault. on April 22nd; they failed to take it. the first time, losing 80 men, a. mountain gun, and 68 rifles. And then,. they called in the aircraft. These. nomads had never seen an airplane in. their lives. There wasn't even a word. in the Tibetan language to describe it. They saw a flying metal machine. dropping things from the sky into the. monastery; they had spent their lives. peacefully herding sheep and had no. idea that those things were bombs. At. noon on the 29th, two bombers strafed. and bombed the monastery repeatedly; at. 4:00 AM on the 30th, troops attacked. from three sides, and the entire. monastery was reduced to rubble. Sichuan military records claim they. wiped out 204, killed 311, wounded 80,. and captured 1,613; Air Force records. show that Tu-4 bombers flew 21 sorties. that spring, bombing Litang and several. surrounding monasteries. Of course,. this was just the beginning; by 1958,. the war reached the grasslands of. Qinghai and Gansu, where the iron birds. in the sky were no longer targeting. monasteries, but ordinary fleeing. civilians. Nomadic tribes herded their. livestock toward the south, with. thousands of people and tens of. thousands of animals stretched out in a. long line. Looking down from an. airplane, this was nothing but a large,. slow-moving ground target. Planes. strafed and bombed from the sky; no one. could count how many people died. On. June 1, 1958, the battle report of the. 1st Cavalry Division in Henan County,. Qinghai, claimed to have annihilated. over 1,200 insurgents, yet the same. files stated that over 7,000 were. surrounded, with only 2,000 rifles. seized. Who, then, were the remaining. four or five thousand people? They had. no guns; they were ordinary people. holding prayer wheels and rosaries,. clutching their children. But what. greeted them were the machine guns of. the troops. After the bursts of gunfire. , bodies drifted down the river. A.

Tibetan named Sangye Norbu later wrote. his memoirs, describing the scene on. the grasslands: as far as the eye could. see, there were corpses everywhere,. many of them children, and mothers. lying dead while holding their children. . In Tiechagou, Qinghai, the People's. Liberation Army deployed bombers and. six regiments. So many Tibetans and. livestock died that their bodies rotted. in the gullies; the water flowing from. the mountains stank, and for three. years after the battle, no one dared to. drink it. Among these people, how many. were armed resisters, and how many were. just elderly people, women, and. children following their tribes? Wave. after wave of Tibetan refugees from. Kham fled to Lhasa. The Dalai Lama and. those around him finally realized that. what had happened in the Kham region. would sooner or later happen to them as. well. On March 10, 1959, rumors spread. that the PLA invited the Dalai Lama to. the military district to watch a play,. forbidding him from bringing his guards. . Thousands of Lhasa residents flooded. outside the Norbulingka palace,. surrounding it to prevent him from. leaving, fearing he would fall into a. CCP ambush. On the night of March 17,. the Dalai Lama disguised himself as an. ordinary soldier and left the city. By. dawn on March 20, PLA artillery shells. were raining down on Norbulingka. On. March 28, Zhou Enlai signed a State. Council order announcing the. dissolution of the Tibetan government. From that day on, the CCP officially. tore up the Seventeen-Point Agreement. it had signed and promised to uphold. The Dalai Lama escaped in time,. entering India on March 31. On April 18. , he issued a statement saying that the. agreement had been imposed on Tibet. under the threat of force, and now,. even the CCP itself no longer abided by. it. According to official Chinese. statistics, from 1956 to 1962, the PLA. mobilized 235,000 troops from eight. military regions and conducted over. 10,000 aircraft sorties. The number of. so-called "eliminated" Tibetans was at. least 347,000, accounting for 16%of the. total Tibetan population at the time. In Qinghai province alone, more than. 108,000 people were arrested between. 1958 and 1960. In Qinghai’s detention. centers, over 80,000 of the imprisoned. Tibetans died, a death rate as high as. 54%. Conditions in detention centers in. other regions were similar, with death. rates exceeding half. Compared to 1957,. the population in the Tibetan regions. had decreased by 44%, and the. population in the Golok area had. dropped by 35%—all according to these. official statistics. In 1982, the. Qinghai provincial government itself. exonerated those who had been labeled. as "rebels" back then, rehabilitating a. total of more than 78,000 people, a. proportion as high as 92%. In other. words, the CCP itself admitted that. among the so-called "rebels" it had. struck and eliminated back then, more. than nine out of every ten cases were. wrong. In May 1962, the Panchen Lama. submitted a report to Zhou Enlai, later. known as the "70,000-Character Petition. ." You must realize the Panchen was. supported by the CCP; even he couldn't. stand it anymore. He stated that before. the reforms, Tibet had over 2,500. temples, but after the reforms, only 70. remained, a reduction of 97%. There. were originally 110,000 monks, now only. 7,000 remain, a reduction of 93%. Every. region arrested at least 10,000 people; in some places, the majority of the. male population was locked up. In. Qinghai, people starved to death, with. daily rations only a few ounces; some. had to survive on roots and tree bark. After Mao Zedong read it, his reaction. was the same as when he saw Peng. Dehuai’s report on the border issues,. calling it a "poisonous arrow shot at. the Party." Because of this letter, the. Panchen was denounced. In 1968, he was. thrown into Qincheng Prison, held until. 1977, and after his release, he was. under house arrest until 1982, finally. returning to Shigatse in January 1989. In a public speech, he stated that. Tibet's sacrifice over the past 30. years had been greater than what had. been gained. Five days later, he died. suddenly at the age of 50. The CCP has. two narratives prepared for Tibet. The. first is the so-called "since ancient. times" argument, which I just explained. . The second is that pre-liberation. Tibet was a feudal serfdom system where. religion and politics were unified. 95%. of the people were serfs and slaves,. and serf owners would flay human skin. for thangkas and use human bones for. ritual objects, with an average life. expectancy of only 35.5 years. After. the CCP's 1959 reforms, millions of. serfs rose up to become masters of. their own destiny. In 2019, a "Serf. Liberation Memorial Hall" opened in.

Lhasa, featuring a sculpture group. called "Serf Rage" made in 1975. After. finishing the exhibit, you are left. feeling that the past was nothing short. of hell. You must thank the Communist. Party and thank the People's Liberation. Army. So, do these so-called human skin. thangkas and human bone ritual objects. actually exist? Objectively speaking,. they do. If you understand Tibetan. Buddhism, you know these are no. different in essence from the sarira. relics worshipped in Han Chinese. Buddhism. For example, the Kapala is. made from a human skull, the Kangling. is a trumpet made from a human thigh. bone, and there are bone drums; these. are all Tantric ritual objects, with. bones coming from deceased. practitioners. The Tibetan tradition is. sky burial, where the body is offered. to vultures, and bones are offered to. temples to be crafted into ritual. objects. In their view, this is an act. of immeasurable merit, and one that is. voluntarily pledged during their. lifetime. In 1964, the Communist. government held an exhibition in. Beijing displaying ritual objects taken. from monasteries, falsely claiming they. were tools used by serf-owners to. torture serfs. This was used to. demonize Tibetan Buddhism and Tibet, a. tactic that was repeated countless. times during the Cultural Revolution. Furthermore, the term "serf" itself is. problematic. In Tibetan, such people. were called "mi-ser," and their status. was fundamentally different from that. of a slave. They had their own land,. could accumulate property, and could. convert their labor obligations into a. cash payment for their lord, which was. known as "mi-ral." Once that was paid,. they were free to leave, whether to. engage in business, join the military,. or farm elsewhere. Many later. Tibetologists have argued that "serf" is fundamentally a misleading Chinese. translation; in reality, they were. simply peasants. It is true that Tibet. was a hierarchical, impoverished, and. medieval society ruled by religion, a. fact that need not be denied, and the. Dalai Lama has never denied it either. However, one should consider what. mainland China was like before 1949. Was it really any better? It was. nothing but warlords fighting for power. . In 1942, two or three million people. starved to death in Henan. The CCP was. constantly under pressure, and even the. archaic practice of foot-binding had. not been completely eradicated in. society. If you use the backwardness of. a mid-20 th-century inland plateau. society to justify an invasion, then by. that same logic, couldn't British. colonization of India or the Japanese. invasion of China also be rationalized? Besides, according to the logic of. institutional superiority, the current. Tibetan government-in-exile has long. since achieved the separation of church. and state, even a separation of powers,. and public debate is permitted in their. parliament. This is far more open than. Tibet today, so why would the CCP. refuse to be replaced by a better. system? Moreover, Tibet was not. standing still; they were also. reforming. Even without the CCP. invasion, Tibet today would have long. since surpassed its former self. As. early as 1913, the 13th Dalai Lama. included in his proclamation a clause. to abolish the death penalty and. prohibit any physical punishments like. amputation. Therefore, Tibetans can. rightfully be proud to say they were. one of the first nations in the world. to abolish the death penalty. The 13th. Dalai Lama also established English. schools, built telegraph and postal. services, and by the 1920s, Lhasa. already had a small hydroelectric. station. They even attempted to build a. modern army, although they did not. succeed. In the early 1950s, the young. 14th Dalai Lama—the same one I later. met who received the Nobel Peace Prize. —established a reform committee to. reduce debts for farmers and reform. rent. He wanted to reclaim parts of the. noble estates to redistribute to the. farmers. This initiative ultimately. failed; partly because the nobles and. monasteries were unwilling, but. surprisingly, the CCP cadres stationed. in Lhasa were also opposed to it. Because the reform they demanded had to. be led by the Party. If you Tibetans. reformed it yourselves, and succeeded,. the Party would have no reason to " liberate" you. This is the most ironic. part of the entire narrative. surrounding the "liberation of serfs." So, what exactly is the relationship. between the CCP and Tibet? Having spent. these days in Dharamshala, a few words. kept coming to my mind: colony and. colonizer. You can take the textbook. definition of colonialism and compare. it point by point. The first point: a.

foreign regime conquers by force. Indeed, in 1950 they took Chamdo, and. in 1959 they took Lhasa. The second. point: settling migrants to alter the. population. If we look at the 2020. census, the Han population in the Tibet. Autonomous Region has doubled compared. to 20 years ago. And that doesn't even. count the stationed troops and the. transient population. The third point:. resource extraction. The local Julong. copper mine belongs to Zijin Mining. Group. It is planned to reach. production by the end of 2025, with an. annual output of 300,000 to 350,000. tons. The company claims it is the. largest single copper mine to go into. operation globally since 2000. There is. also lithium from Lake Zabuye, with. 2,000 tons of lithium carbonate, and. the Gangtuo hydropower station project. on the Jinsha River, which began. construction last July with a capacity. of 60 to 70 million kilowatts—three. times that of the Three Gorges Dam. The. electricity is mainly sent to the. mainland, and the profits are not. shared with the Tibetans. In February. 2024, Tibetans in Dege, Sichuan, knelt. on the ground to petition against the. Gangtuo hydropower project on the. Jinsha River, which would submerge four. monasteries; as a result, over a. thousand people were arrested. The. fourth point: economic dependence. The. total fiscal expenditure for the Tibet. Autonomous Region in 2025 is 310. billion yuan. Their own revenue is only. 31.8 billion, with 239 billion in. central government transfer payments. 82%of the money comes from Beijing,. which wants you to rely on them so you. cannot survive without them. However,. this money, once allocated from Beijing. to Tibet, passes through infrastructure. projects, state-owned enterprises, Han. contractors, and Han skilled workers,. effectively flowing right back to the. mainland. Yet, this so-called. construction and development in Tibet. is packaged as a national benevolence. And, of course, one must be profoundly. grateful for this "gift." Regarding. cultural assimilation, in February 2023. , UN special rapporteurs issued a. statement saying that approximately one. million Tibetan children have been sent. to technical schools and forcibly. separated from their families. The term. used was "forced assimilation." On. March 12th of this year, the CCP passed. the "Law on Promoting National Unity." We will find another time to discuss. this in detail. Starting in 2023,. official Chinese English documents have. actually changed the English word " Tibet" to the pinyin "Xizang." It's no. wonder people say Tibet will sooner or. later become "West Hong Kong." The. international organization Freedom. House scores every country in the world. annually out of 100 points. Tibet has. received a score of zero for three. consecutive years—2024, 2025, and. 2026—making it the least free place. on earth, scoring lower even than North. Korea and mainland China. Since 2009,. 159 Tibetans inside China have. protested CCP oppression through. self-immolation, 26 of whom are still. unaccounted for. On July 2nd of this. year, a Tibetan man named Lobsang. Tsultrim set himself on fire in front. of the UN headquarters in New York. During this trip to Dharamsala, every. time I saw a poster of him on the. street, I would stop to mourn. So I. believe that, to be honest, the. situation of Tibetans today is not much. better than that of the serfs half a. century ago. In old Tibet, serfs could. leave after fulfilling their duties, do. business, or serve a different lord. Children in monasteries could still. learn the Tibetan language, but today. children are sent to technical schools. at age six. Centuries-old temples must. hang portraits of Xi Jinping, and. people are forced to study so-called " socialist core values." Even keeping a. photo of the Dalai Lama in your home. can get you a prison sentence. Passports for traveling abroad are. basically impossible to obtain. The. mountain trails used for escaping have. also been completely sealed off. Old. Tibet shackled their standard of living. , but today’s shackles bind their. language, their thoughts, and their. faith. As well as the future of the. entire nation. Since elementary school,. we have often seen the term "Century of. Humiliation" in our history textbooks. From 1840 to 1949, textbooks told us. foreign armies invaded, burned the Old. Summer Palace, forced us to pay. reparations, and the Eight-Nation. Alliance entered Beijing. Every one of. us was taught that we must never forget. . But if you apply the same standard to. the Tibetan people, look at what you. find. In 1904, the British army entered. Lhasa; in 1910, the Qing army entered. Lhasa; in 1950, the PLA entered Tibet,.

followed by over 60 years of rule,. destroying temples and burning. monasteries. This has also been a. century for this nation, and it still. hasn't ended to this day. A people want. to govern themselves, want to speak. their own language and recite their own. scriptures, want their children to know. who they are, and don't want to have a. foreign regime's gun pointed at their. heads. This desire is the same as the. 1911 Xinhai Revolution when the Chinese. overthrew the Qing Dynasty, or the. Taiwanese fighting for elections in the. 1980s, right? It is essentially the. same path as the Hong Kongers taking to. the streets against the extradition. bill in 2019, and the Ukrainians. holding their ground in the war today. If you support national independence. and freedom, there is no reason to be. indifferent to the plight of the. Tibetans. Today you might say Tibetans. are separatists unworthy of sympathy,. but tomorrow someone will label you a. foreign agent, also unworthy of. compassion. So, seeing those elders in. Dharamsala who have been in exile for. 60 years unable to return home, and. seeing the young Tibetans born in India. who have only seen Lhasa in photos, my. heart felt truly mixed. Why must the. CCP treat people this way? It's. actually quite simple: they treat all. Chinese people this way; the Tibetans. are just under tighter control. Look at. how the CCP deals with all its critics. and dissenters; the exiled Tibetans are. called the "Dalai Clique" by the CCP, a. tool of Western anti-China forces. It. is true that the CIA funded Tibetan. armed resistance during the Cold War; that was part of the free world. opposing the communist camp, having. nothing to do with Tibetan independence. . After Nixon's visit in 1972, the CIA. cut off all these links. The Americans. did help the Tibetans, and so they. became so-called "running dogs." But. Americans also helped the CCP for 40. years, right? Helping China with reform. , opening up, and becoming strong—. does that mean all Chinese people are. American running dogs? When Liu Xiaobo. received the Nobel Prize, the Global. Times editorialized that the prize had. become a political tool serving Western. interests. Xinhua News Agency even said. it was a reward from the West. Nationalists online hurled insults at. Liu Xiaobo, calling him a traitor at. every turn. Yet what Liu Xiaobo. advocated for was constitutionalism,. freedom of speech, and judicial. independence. These things and the. Tibetan desire to shed CCP rule and. practice democratic autonomy are. essentially the same goal, but in the. eyes of the CCP, whoever wants freedom. is a traitor. Whoever wants freedom is. a separatist, whoever wants freedom is. a foreign agent. I have said in my. previous programs that a nation is. imagined, relying on a common language,. printed materials, memory, and. narratives. The most important slogan. of the CCP in recent years is to "forge. a strong sense of community for the. Chinese nation." To put it bluntly, it. is about reconstructing an imagined. community, wiping out the distinct. cultures, traditions, languages,. beliefs, and historical memories of. Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongolians, and even. Hong Kongers and Taiwanese, and. formatting them all. In fact, they have. always been doing exactly this in the. past. For example, you don't know what. happened in Lhasa in 1959, but do you. know what happened in Henan in that. same year? Most Chinese people don't. know either. Or, you might not know. about the martial law in Lhasa in 1989,. but don't young people in China today. also not know about what happened in. Tiananmen, Beijing, three months later? The same regime is using the same. method to erase all national memories. They only need you to remember to. listen to the Party, follow the Party,. and be grateful to the Party; that is. enough. For many years, the demands of. the Tibetan people have actually been. the so-called "Middle Way." They do not. seek independence; they only want. genuine autonomy. And this is precisely. what the CCP promised in black and. white back then. The Dalai Lama has. been mentioning this appeal since 1988,. which is nearly 40 years now, but let's. look at Hong Kong today. "One Country,. Two Systems" has long since failed. Everyone has come to realize that no. matter what path you propose, as long. as it is not the path of the CCP's. autocratic rule, they will not tolerate. it. I will leave the conversation here. for this episode. Thank you all for. watching. As for my experiences in. Dharamsala, the vast amount of. first-hand footage I filmed, as well as. my thoughts on the Dalai Lama and the. issue of reincarnation, I will make. more episodes in the future for you to.

watch. Thank you all for watching this. episode. Welcome to subscribe, like,. and turn on the notification bell. I am. Gong Zishen. See you in the next. episode.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析西藏與歷代中原王朝的政治與宗教關係，釐清「自古以來」論述的歷史爭議。
  • 完整梳理1911年至1951年間西藏發行貨幣、辦理外交等實質獨立狀態的具體實踐。
  • 以作者親訪達蘭薩拉的田野觀察視角切入，提供跳脫傳統單一敘事的多元歷史維度。

摘要

從觀光熱潮到流亡重鎮：達蘭薩拉的見聞

作者指出，當代大眾前往西藏旅遊已形成風潮，但多數人對達賴喇嘛流亡印度及1959年拉薩事件的歷史背景缺乏了解。為探尋西藏的過往與現狀，作者親赴印度北部山城達蘭薩拉（又稱「小拉薩」），實地走訪聚集數萬藏人與流亡政府的所在地，並藉此檢視中共關於「西藏自古屬於中國」以及「十七條協議」等歷史敘事。

解構「自古以來」：唐元明清與西藏的真實互動

針對官方宣稱西藏「自古以來」屬於中國的論調，作者回顧了歷代歷史。唐代時期，吐蕃帝國實力足以與唐朝分庭抗禮，拉薩大昭寺前立於823年的《唐蕃會盟碑》便明文記載兩國各自劃定邊界、互為對等國家。元代蒙古人統治時，雙方形成提供庇護與福田的「供施關係」，並非主權管轄；若依征服邏輯，反而是中原與西藏同遭蒙古征服。明朝從未在西藏駐軍或徵稅，而清朝雖於18世紀擊退準噶爾後設置駐藏大臣並推行金瓶掣籤，但事務劃歸理藩院處理，屬於滿洲大汗對藩屬的保護關係，非等同於內地十八省的直接統治。

實質獨立的四十年：1911至1951年的西藏主權實踐
